newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW-Northern Rock sticks to mortgage guns.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Northern Rock sticks to mortgage guns.

text.p: The Northern Rock Building Society, which floats as a bank on October 1, said on Tuesday it would stick to what it does best -- mortgages -- firmly rejecting more fashionable diversification.

The Society, in its last set of results before it comes to market, raised pre-tax profits 10.2 percent to 97 million stg, before non-recurring costs, and saw its assets climb 13.6 percent to 14.6 billion.

"What we're very good at is mortgage lending funded predominantly by cash deposits," said Northern Rock executive director Adam Applegarth in an interview. "That's what we're good at, other things we tend not to be so good at."
He noted that Northern Rock's forays into estate agency and the independent financial advice (IFA) market had not been successful.
The society said on Tuesday it would close its small IFA unit Northern Rock Financial Services and sell its asset management unit which has only around 30 million stg of assets.

Applegarth said new entrants to the mortgage market such as supermarket banks were being watched but he doubted they would be able to undercut current mortgage lenders for too long unless they want to pay up for market share and make huge losses in the short-term.
"New aspirants in the mortgage market are going to find it a very expensive business," he said.
Applegarth said Northern Rock currently had no acquisitions in mind, noting that the Society would lose its five-year statutory protection against takeover if it buys another financial institution.

"I suspect it would have to be a sufficiently large acquisition to justify giving up the protection but we have nothing in mind," Applegarth added. "We have a track record of organic growth and that's what we plan carry on delivering."

The Society was cautious about the housing market and Applegarth said it is taking time for buoyancy in the South East of England to ripple out elsewhere although there are some positive signs in East Anglia and the South West of England.
"I think the second half of the year will see buoyant lending volumes generally in the market and I expect Northern Rock to get its share of that," Applegarth said.
Northern Rock, which prides itself on being a low-cost provider, again reported a lower cost/income ratio -- down to 30.9 percent compared to 31.5 at the half way stage last year.

Applegarth said the society has no particular cost/income ratio target. "If we can get down to the mid-twenties then that's a good start -- the answer is we'll keep hammering away at it and see what happens."
Northern Rock also wants to see its Tier one capital ratio edge lower from its current level of 8.7 percent though he declined to set a level.
"It will nudge down as we burn it off by growing the business and returning dividends to shareholders."
